entries.meaning: To break food up with your teeth before swallowing it. ---
examples: Chew your food slowly — it helps digestion.
The puppy chewed the corner off my shoe.
She sat chewing gum and staring out the window.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (chew your food), intransitive (chew slowly)

entries.meaning: To make food or drink go down your throat. ---
examples: Swallow the pill with plenty of water.
He swallowed the last bite and stood up.
She winced, swallowing the bitter medicine.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (swallow a pill), intransitive (it hurts to swallow)

entries.meaning: To eat something noisily and steadily, usually a crunchy snack. ---
examples: The kids munch popcorn through the whole movie.
He munched on carrot sticks while he waited.
I could hear someone munching chips behind me.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (munch popcorn), intransitive (munch on chips)
entries.contrast: Verbs ending in -ch add -es in the third person: he munches.

entries.meaning: To eat something quickly and hungrily. ---
examples: Teenagers devour whatever is in the fridge.
He devoured two plates of pasta in ten minutes.
The cake had been devoured before I got a slice.

entries.meaning: To eat small amounts of food between meals. ---
examples: I snack too much when I study.
We snacked on almonds during the drive.
She has been snacking all afternoon.
entries.contrast: Takes on before the food: snack on nuts, never 'snack nuts'.

entries.meaning: To eat a large, festive meal with great enjoyment. ---
examples: Every November they feast on turkey and pie.
We feasted until nobody could move.
The guests were feasting while the cook rested.
entries.contrast: Takes on: feast on lobster.

entries.meaning: To eat dinner, especially in a restaurant or in a formal setting. ---
examples: They dine out every Friday.
We dined on the terrace as the sun went down.
We were dining when the power went out.
entries.contrast: The silent -e disappears before -ing: dining with one n.

entries.meaning: To break food down in the stomach so the body can use it. ---
examples: Babies cannot digest solid food yet.
He never fully digested that fried chicken.
Sit still for a while — your body is digesting lunch.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (dy-JEST); the noun a digest on the first.

entries.meaning: To eat or drink something, especially in a measured amount. ---
examples: Americans consume a lot of sugar.
He consumed three liters of water that day.
The label shows how many calories you are consuming.

entries.meaning: To eat or drink something with a loud sucking noise. ---
examples: Please don't slurp your soup at the table.
He slurped the last of the noodles.
Someone behind me was slurping iced coffee.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (slurp your soup), intransitive (stop slurping)

entries.meaning: To swallow a drink or food quickly in large mouthfuls. ---
examples: Don't gulp your milk like that.
He gulped the water and asked for more.
She was gulping air after the run.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (gulp your milk), intransitive (he gulped nervously)

entries.meaning: To drink a whole drink quickly without stopping, in informal speech. ---
examples: College kids chug soda at parties.
He chugged a bottle of water after practice.
They were chugging lemonade in the heat.
entries.contrast: The g doubles: chugged, chugging.

entries.meaning: To brown bread or nuts with dry heat, or to raise a glass in someone's honor. ---
examples: Toast the bread while I fry the eggs.
We stood and toasted the newlyweds.
She is toasting almonds for the salad.

entries.meaning: To satisfy your thirst with a drink. ---
examples: Nothing quenches thirst like cold water.
The lemonade quenched our thirst in seconds.
He drank soda after soda without quenching anything.
entries.contrast: Almost always with thirst; -ch takes -es: quenches.

entries.meaning: To suffer or die from a lack of food. ---
examples: I'm starving — when is dinner?
Whole villages starved that winter.
He has starved himself on that diet for weeks.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (starve yourself), intransitive (the cattle starved)
entries.contrast: In everyday speech I'm starving just means 'very hungry'.

entries.meaning: To go without food for a period of time, often for religious or medical reasons. ---
examples: Many people fast during Ramadan.
She fasted for twelve hours before the blood test.
He has been fasting since sunrise.
entries.contrast: Spelled like the adjective fast 'quick', but the meanings are unrelated.

entries.meaning: To limit what you eat in order to lose weight. ---
examples: She diets every January.
He dieted for months before the wedding.
I'm dieting, so no cake for me.
entries.contrast: Stress is on the first syllable, so the t is not doubled: dieted, dieting.

entries.meaning: To want a particular food or drink very badly. ---
examples: Pregnant women often crave strange foods.
I craved salt for days after the flu.
He has been craving his mother's soup.

entries.meaning: To be unable to breathe because food or drink is blocking your throat. ---
examples: Cut the grapes so the baby doesn't choke.
He choked on a fish bone at dinner.
She started choking and someone slapped her back.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (the smoke choked us), intransitive (he choked on a bone)
entries.contrast: Takes on before the food: choke on a bone.

entries.meaning: To bring food up from the stomach and out through the mouth. ---
examples: The bad oysters made him vomit.
She vomited twice during the night.
He was pale and vomiting by morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (vomit blood), intransitive (he vomited twice)
entries.contrast: First-syllable stress, so the t is not doubled: vomited, vomiting.

entries.meaning: To let air come up noisily from the stomach through the mouth. ---
examples: It's rude to burp at the table.
The baby burped and fell asleep.
She is burping him after his bottle.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (burp the baby), intransitive (he burped loudly)

entries.meaning: To let saliva run out of your mouth, often because food smells or looks good. ---
examples: Dogs drool when they smell bacon.
The baby drooled all over his bib.
We stood drooling in front of the bakery window.

entries.meaning: To fill a food tightly with a mixture, or to fill yourself with too much food. ---
examples: Stuff the peppers with rice and ground beef.
She stuffed the turkey the night before.
We were stuffed after the third course.
entries.contrast: The participle is an everyday adjective: I'm stuffed means 'I've eaten too much'.

entries.meaning: To show someone to a place to sit, especially in a restaurant. ---
examples: The host will seat you in a moment.
They seated us by the window.
Please wait to be seated.

entries.meaning: To provide and serve food for an event. ---
examples: Who is going to cater the wedding?
A local deli catered the office party.
They have been catering events for twenty years.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cater a wedding), intransitive (they cater to vegans)
entries.contrast: With to it means 'serve someone's tastes': the menu caters to vegetarians.

entries.meaning: To get food or a meal ready. ---
examples: I'll prepare the salad while you grill.
She prepared dinner for twelve.
The chef is preparing a tasting menu.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: preparing.

entries.meaning: To prepare food using heat. ---
examples: He cooks dinner on weeknights.
She cooked rice and beans for everyone.
Something is cooking — I can smell it.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cook dinner), intransitive (the rice is cooking)

entries.meaning: To heat a liquid until it bubbles, or to cook food in bubbling water. ---
examples: Boil the water before you add the pasta.
I boiled two eggs for breakfast.
The soup has been boiling for ten minutes.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (boil the eggs), intransitive (the water is boiling)

entries.meaning: To cook food in hot oil or fat. ---
examples: Don't fry the fish too long.
He fried onions in butter.
She is frying bacon for the sandwiches.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (fry the fish), intransitive (the onions are frying)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie- in fries and fried, but stays in frying.

entries.meaning: To cook food on a rack over direct heat, usually outdoors. ---
examples: We grill burgers every Fourth of July.
He grilled chicken and corn.
They were grilling in the backyard when it rained.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (grill the burgers), intransitive (we grilled all afternoon)

entries.meaning: To cook meat, vegetables, or nuts in an oven or over a fire. ---
examples: Roast the vegetables at four hundred degrees.
She roasted a chicken with lemon.
The coffee beans are roasted locally.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (roast a chicken), intransitive (the beef is roasting)

entries.meaning: To cook food over boiling water, using the vapor. ---
examples: Steam the broccoli for four minutes.
I steamed the dumplings instead of frying them.
The rice is steaming on the back burner.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (steam the broccoli), intransitive (the rice is steaming)

entries.meaning: To cook something gently in liquid kept just below boiling. ---
examples: Let the sauce simmer for an hour.
She simmered the stock all afternoon.
The beans have been simmering since noon.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (simmer the sauce), intransitive (let it simmer)

entries.meaning: To fry food quickly in a little hot fat, stirring as it cooks. ---
examples: Sauté the garlic before you add the tomatoes.
He sautéed mushrooms in olive oil.
She is sautéing onions for the soup.
entries.contrast: A French loanword: American recipes keep the accent — sautéed, sautéing.

entries.meaning: To cook food gently in barely simmering liquid. ---
examples: Poach the eggs for three minutes.
She poached salmon in white wine.
He likes his eggs poached, not fried.
entries.contrast: -ch takes -es: poaches.

entries.meaning: To heat or cook food in a microwave oven. ---
examples: Microwave it for ninety seconds.
He microwaved last night's pizza.
She is microwaving a bowl of soup.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: microwaving.

entries.meaning: To heat food again after it has cooled. ---
examples: Reheat the sauce over low heat.
I reheated the leftovers for lunch.
The pasta is reheating in the oven.

entries.meaning: To make food or drink moderately hot. ---
examples: Warm the milk before you add the yeast.
She warmed the rolls in the oven.
He is warming soup on the stove.

entries.meaning: To make something hot, especially food or liquid. ---
examples: Heat the oil until it shimmers.
I heated the leftovers in a pan.
The skillet is heating now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (heat the oil), intransitive (the oven is heating)

entries.meaning: To make food or drink cold, usually in a refrigerator. ---
examples: Chill the wine for an hour.
She chilled the dough overnight.
The dessert is chilling in the fridge.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (chill the wine), intransitive (the dough chills overnight)

entries.meaning: To keep food cold in a refrigerator so that it stays fresh. ---
examples: Refrigerate the sauce after opening.
I refrigerated the soup overnight.
Fresh pasta must be refrigerated, not left out.

entries.meaning: To let frozen food warm up until it is no longer frozen. ---
examples: Defrost the chicken in the fridge, not on the counter.
She defrosted the shrimp under cold water.
The steaks are defrosting on a plate.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (defrost the chicken), intransitive (the steaks defrosted)

entries.meaning: To become unfrozen, or to let frozen food do so. ---
examples: Let the fish thaw before you cook it.
The berries thawed in about an hour.
The turkey is still thawing.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (thaw the turkey), intransitive (the berries thawed)
entries.contrast: Rhymes with law: the final w is not pronounced.

entries.meaning: To soak food in a seasoned liquid before cooking it. ---
examples: Marinate the beef for at least an hour.
He marinated the chicken in yogurt and spices.
The ribs have been marinating since morning.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (marinate the beef), intransitive (let it marinate)

entries.meaning: To scatter small amounts of something over food. ---
examples: Sprinkle sugar over the berries.
He sprinkled cheese on the pasta.
She is sprinkling salt on the fries.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: sprinkling.

entries.meaning: To decorate a dish or a drink with a small piece of food. ---
examples: Garnish the soup with parsley.
The bartender garnished the drink with a lime wedge.
Each plate was garnished with mint.
entries.contrast: False friend: English garnish is a decoration, not Russian гарнир — that is a side dish. And -sh takes -es: garnishes.

entries.meaning: To pour a thin stream of liquid slowly over food. ---
examples: Drizzle olive oil over the salad.
She drizzled honey on the yogurt.
He is drizzling melted chocolate on the cake.

entries.meaning: To put something on the surface of a dish as a finishing layer. ---
examples: Top the pie with whipped cream.
They topped the burger with a fried egg.
The sundae came topped with nuts.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: topped, topping.

entries.meaning: To spread butter on bread or over a cooking dish. ---
examples: Butter the pan before you pour the batter.
He buttered four slices of toast.
She is buttering rolls for the table.
entries.contrast: First-syllable stress, so no doubling: buttered, buttering.

entries.meaning: To cut food into small cubes. ---
examples: Dice the potatoes so they cook evenly.
He diced an onion and a carrot.
She is dicing peppers for the salsa.

entries.meaning: To chop food into very small pieces. ---
examples: Mince two cloves of garlic.
She minced fresh ginger for the marinade.
He is mincing herbs with a heavy knife.
entries.contrast: In American English chopped meat is ground beef, not 'mince'.

entries.meaning: To remove the skin from a fruit or vegetable. ---
examples: Peel the carrots before you grate them.
He peeled five potatoes.
She is peeling an orange for the kids.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (peel a potato), intransitive (the skin peels off easily)

entries.meaning: To rub food against a rough surface so it breaks into small shreds. ---
examples: Grate some parmesan over the pasta.
She grated a whole block of cheese.
He is grating carrots for the salad.
entries.contrast: Sounds exactly like great; the -e drops before -ing: grating.

entries.meaning: To crush cooked food into a soft mass. ---
examples: Mash the potatoes with butter and milk.
He mashed a banana for the baby.
She is mashing avocado for the guacamole.
entries.contrast: -sh takes -es: mashes.

entries.meaning: To beat cream or eggs quickly until they are light and thick. ---
examples: Whip the cream until it holds peaks.
She whipped the egg whites by hand.
He is whipping butter and sugar together.
entries.contrast: The p doubles: whipped, whipping — as in whipped cream.

entries.meaning: To mix or beat ingredients rapidly with a wire tool or a fork. ---
examples: Whisk the eggs with a little milk.
He whisked the sauce until it was smooth.
She is whisking batter for pancakes.

entries.meaning: To make a liquid flow from one container into another. ---
examples: Pour the milk slowly.
He poured everyone a glass of wine.
She is pouring coffee for the table.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (pour the milk), intransitive (pour from the jug)
entries.contrast: Rhymes with more; the sound-alike pore is a tiny hole in the skin.

entries.meaning: To lift food out with a spoon or a deep utensil. ---
examples: Scoop the ice cream into bowls.
He scooped the seeds out of the pumpkin.
She is scooping rice onto each plate.

entries.meaning: To fill a glass or a container again. ---
examples: Waiters here refill your coffee for free.
She refilled my water twice.
He is refilling the pitcher.
entries.contrast: The verb is stressed on the second syllable (ree-FIL); the noun a refill on the first.

entries.meaning: To leave tea or herbs in hot water so that the flavor comes out. ---
examples: Steep the tea for three minutes.
He steeped the leaves too long and it turned bitter.
The tea has been steeping since you left.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (steep the tea), intransitive (let it steep)
entries.contrast: Also a common adjective meaning 'sharply sloped': a steep hill.

entries.meaning: To make a liquid weaker by adding water to it. ---
examples: Dilute the syrup with cold water.
He diluted the juice for the children.
The soup tasted diluted after all that broth.

entries.meaning: To leave food or dishes in liquid for a long time. ---
examples: Soak the beans overnight.
She soaked the rice for twenty minutes.
The pans are soaking in the sink.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (soak the beans), intransitive (the rice soaks for an hour)

entries.meaning: To wash something quickly with clean water. ---
examples: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear.
He rinsed the lettuce twice.
She is rinsing the plates before loading them.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: rinsing.

entries.meaning: To clean something with water, usually with soap. ---
examples: Wash your hands before you cook.
He washed the dishes after dinner.
She is washing grapes at the sink.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (wash the dishes), intransitive (wash before dinner)
entries.contrast: -sh takes -es: washes.

entries.meaning: To take dishes and food off a table. ---
examples: Let's clear the table before dessert.
She cleared the plates while we talked.
He is clearing the last of the glasses.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (clear the table), intransitive (we cleared up after dinner)

entries.meaning: To remove dirt or food from something. ---
examples: Clean the grill while it's still warm.
He cleaned the kitchen after the party.
She is cleaning the counters.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (clean the grill), intransitive (she cleans on Saturdays)

entries.meaning: To rub a surface with a cloth to clean or dry it. ---
examples: Wipe the table, please.
He wiped his mouth with a napkin.
She is wiping down the counter.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: wiping.

entries.meaning: To rub something hard with a brush or cloth to clean it. ---
examples: Scrub the potatoes under cold water.
He scrubbed the burnt pan for ten minutes.
She is scrubbing the cutting board.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (scrub the pan), intransitive (scrub harder)
entries.contrast: The b doubles: scrubbed, scrubbing.

entries.meaning: To remove the water from something. ---
examples: Dry the lettuce before you dress it.
He washed and dried every glass.
The herbs are drying by the window.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (dry the glasses), intransitive (the herbs dried in a week)
entries.contrast: The -y becomes -ie- in dries and dried, but stays in drying.

entries.meaning: To put enough of something into a container to make it full. ---
examples: Fill the pot with cold water.
She filled our glasses to the top.
He is filling the kettle.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (fill the pot), intransitive (the restaurant fills up by seven)
entries.contrast: Takes with for the contents: fill the glass with water.

entries.meaning: To keep vegetables in vinegar or salty water so that they last and taste sour. ---
examples: You can pickle almost any vegetable.
He pickled a jar of cucumbers.
She is pickling red onions for the tacos.
entries.contrast: The final -e drops before -ing: pickling.

entries.meaning: To draw liquid or a piece of food into your mouth with your lips. ---
examples: Don't suck the juice straight out of the box.
She sucked her soda through a straw.
He was sucking on a cough drop.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (suck the juice out), intransitive (suck on a candy)
entries.contrast: With candy or a straw it takes on: suck on a lozenge.

entries.meaning: To turn food over quickly so that the other side cooks. ---
examples: Flip the pancakes when they bubble.
He flipped the burgers one by one.
She is flipping an omelet in the pan.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (flip the pancakes), intransitive (the burger flipped onto the coals)
entries.contrast: The p doubles: flipped, flipping.

entries.meaning: To heat an oven to the right temperature before the food goes in. ---
examples: Preheat the oven to three hundred fifty degrees.
I preheated the oven while I mixed the batter.
The oven is still preheating.

entries.meaning: To cook food with strong heat coming from above, as in an American oven. ---
examples: Broil the fish for four minutes.
She broiled the cheese until it bubbled.
The chicken is broiling now.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (broil the fish), intransitive (the chicken is broiling)
entries.contrast: American broil (heat from above) is what the British call grill.

entries.meaning: To become less hot, or to make something less hot. ---
examples: Let the pie cool before you cut it.
The soup cooled while we talked.
The cookies are cooling on a rack.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cool the syrup), intransitive (let the pie cool)

entries.meaning: To add salt to food. ---
examples: Salt the water before the pasta goes in.
He salted the fries twice.
She is salting the meat before it goes on the grill.
entries.contrast: The l is pronounced: SAWLT, not 'sawt'.

entries.meaning: To make food or drink taste sweeter. ---
examples: Sweeten the tea with honey instead of sugar.
She sweetened the sauce with a little maple syrup.
This yogurt is sweetened with fruit.

entries.meaning: To cook food for too long, so that it turns dry or mushy.
examples: Don't overcook the shrimp.
He overcooked the pasta again.
The steak was badly overcooked.
